title: Surface Areas and Volumes
summary: Chapter 12 of NCERT Class 10 Mathematics covers Areas Related to Circles. This chapter explores the calculation of areas of sectors, segments, and combinations of plane figures involving circles. Students learn to find areas of sectors using the formula (θ/360) × πr² and segments by subtracting the area of triangles from sectors. The chapter also covers the area of combinations of circles with other shapes like triangles, rectangles, and squares. Key concepts include the relationship between arc length and sector area, the difference between minor and major segments, and the application of these concepts in real-world problems. The chapter builds upon students' understanding of circles and mensuration from previous classes.

sections.heading: Introduction to Circles and Related Areas
sections.para: A circle is a collection of points in a plane that are at a constant distance from a fixed point called the center. The constant distance is called the radius. The area of a circle is given by πr² where r is the radius. A sector of a circle is the portion enclosed by two radii and an arc. The area of a sector is proportional to the central angle subtended by the arc. A segment of a circle is the region bounded by a chord and the arc subtended by that chord. Understanding these fundamental concepts is essential before proceeding to more complex calculations involving combinations of figures.
points: A circle is defined as the locus of points equidistant from a fixed center point
The area of a circle is πr² where r represents the radius
A sector is formed by two radii and the included arc
The area of a sector is proportional to its central angle
A segment is the region between a chord and its corresponding arc
The circumference of a circle is 2πr or πd where d is the diameter
The length of an arc is (θ/360) × 2πr where θ is the central angle
The area of a sector is (θ/360) × πr²

keyTerms.meaning: A closed curve where all points are equidistant from a fixed center point
The distance from the center of a circle to any point on its circumference
The region enclosed by two radii and an arc of the circle
The region bounded by a chord and the arc subtended by that chord
A continuous portion of the circumference of a circle
A straight line segment joining any two points on the circumference

sections.trick: Remember 'SAARC' for Sector Area: Sector Area = Arc length × Radius / 2
sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks 1-2 mark questions on basic circle properties and 3-4 mark questions on sector and segment area calculations. Always show step-by-step working with proper substitution of values.

sections.heading: Area of a Sector
sections.para: The area of a sector of a circle is the portion of the circle enclosed by two radii and an arc. The area of a sector is directly proportional to the central angle subtended by the arc. For a circle with radius r and a sector with central angle θ degrees, the area of the sector is given by (θ/360) × πr². This formula is derived from the fact that the area of a full circle (360°) is πr², so the area of a sector is the fraction (θ/360) of the total area. When θ is given in radians, the formula becomes (1/2)r²θ. Students must be comfortable converting between degrees and radians when necessary.
points: The area of a sector is proportional to its central angle
For θ in degrees: Area = (θ/360) × πr²
For θ in radians: Area = (1/2)r²θ
When θ = 360°, the sector becomes the full circle with area πr²
When θ = 180°, the sector is a semicircle with area (1/2)πr²
The area of a sector can also be calculated as (arc length × radius)/2
A sector with θ = 90° is called a quadrant and has area (1/4)πr²
The perimeter of a sector includes the arc length plus two radii

keyTerms.meaning: The angle subtended by an arc at the center of the circle
The relationship where sector area varies directly with the central angle
An alternative unit for measuring angles where 180° = π radians
A sector with central angle of 90 degrees
A sector with central angle of 180 degrees

sections.trick: Remember 'Degree-Denominator': For degree measure, divide by 360; for radians, use half radius squared
sections.examPointer: CBSE commonly asks 3-4 mark questions requiring application of sector area formula. Problems may involve finding area given angle and radius, finding angle given area and radius, or finding radius given area and angle. Always show the formula substitution step.

sections.heading: Area of a Segment
sections.para: A segment of a circle is the region bounded by a chord and the arc subtended by that chord. There are two types of segments: the minor segment (smaller area) and the major segment (larger area). To find the area of a segment, we subtract the area of the corresponding triangle from the area of the sector. For a circle with radius r and central angle θ, the area of the minor segment is given by (θ/360) × πr² - (1/2)r²sinθ. The first term represents the area of the sector, and the second term represents the area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord. For the major segment, we subtract the minor segment area from the total area of the circle.
points: A segment is the region between a chord and its corresponding arc
The area of a minor segment = Area of sector - Area of triangle
The area of a major segment = Area of circle - Area of minor segment
When θ = 180°, the segment becomes a semicircle
When θ = 90°, the segment area is (πr²/4) - (r²/2)
The chord length can be found using 2r sin(θ/2)
The perpendicular distance from center to chord is r cos(θ/2)
For θ > 180°, we calculate the major segment directly

keyTerms.meaning: The smaller region bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc
The larger region bounded by a chord and its corresponding arc
The straight-line distance between two points on the circumference
The shortest distance from the center to the chord
The area of the portion enclosed by two radii and an arc

sections.trick: Remember 'Sector Minus Triangle' for minor segment area calculation
sections.examPointer: CBSE typically asks 4 mark questions on segment area calculations. Problems may involve finding segment area given radius and angle, or finding unknown parameters given segment area. Always clearly show the subtraction of triangle area from sector area.

sections.heading: Area of Combinations of Circles with Other Shapes
sections.para: Many real-world problems involve finding areas of combinations of circles with other plane figures like triangles, rectangles, squares, and other circles. To solve such problems, we need to visualize the given figure and identify the simple shapes that constitute it. The total area is then found by adding or subtracting the areas of these individual shapes. For example, the area of a circle inscribed in a square is found by subtracting the area of the circle from the area of the square. Similarly, the area of a circle circumscribed about a triangle is found by adding the area of the circle to the area of the triangle. Careful identification of overlapping regions is crucial in these calculations.
points: Combinations involve circles with triangles, rectangles, squares, or other circles
Total area is found by adding or subtracting individual shape areas
For a circle inscribed in a square: Area = Square area - Circle area
For a circle circumscribed about a triangle: Area = Triangle area + Circle area
When two circles intersect, find areas of individual circles and subtract overlap
For a circle in a corner of a rectangle: Area = Rectangle area - Circle area
For concentric circles: Area between them = Outer circle - Inner circle
Always identify which parts to add and which to subtract carefully

keyTerms.meaning: A circle that fits inside another shape touching all sides
A circle that passes through all vertices of a polygon
Circles with the same center but different radii
The area common to two or more intersecting shapes
A shape made up of two or more simple geometric figures

sections.trick: Visualize first, then break down: 'See, Split, Solve' for combination problems
sections.examPointer: CBSE commonly asks 4-6 mark questions on areas of combinations. These are typically multi-step problems requiring visualization and careful calculation. Always draw diagrams and show all steps of area calculations for each component shape.

sections.heading: Perimeter of a Sector
sections.para: The perimeter of a sector includes the arc length plus the lengths of the two radii. For a circle with radius r and central angle θ degrees, the perimeter of the sector is given by 2r + (θ/360) × 2πr. The first term represents the two radii, and the second term represents the arc length. When θ is given in radians, the formula becomes 2r + rθ. Understanding perimeter calculations is important for solving problems involving boundaries of circular sectors. Students must be able to distinguish between the perimeter of a sector and the perimeter of a segment, which includes the chord length instead of the two radii.
points: Perimeter of sector = Arc length + 2 × radius
For θ in degrees: Perimeter = 2r + (θ/360) × 2πr
For θ in radians: Perimeter = 2r + rθ
When θ = 180°, perimeter = 2r + πr = r(2 + π)
When θ = 90°, perimeter = 2r + (πr/2) = r(2 + π/2)
Perimeter of segment = Arc length + Chord length
Chord length = 2r sin(θ/2)
Units of perimeter are the same as units of length

keyTerms.meaning: The distance along the curved part of the circumference
The straight-line distance between two points on the circumference
The total distance around the boundary of a shape
An alternative unit for measuring angles where 180° = π radians
The angle subtended by an arc at the center of the circle

sections.trick: Remember 'Two Radii Plus Arc' for sector perimeter calculation
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks 2-3 mark questions on perimeter of sectors. Problems may involve finding perimeter given radius and angle, or finding unknown parameters given perimeter. Always clearly distinguish between sector perimeter and segment perimeter.

sections.heading: Area of Shaded Regions
sections.para: Finding the area of shaded regions is a common application of the concepts learned in this chapter. A shaded region is typically an area enclosed by multiple geometric figures where only a specific portion is shaded. To find the area of a shaded region, we need to identify the shapes that constitute the region and determine whether to add or subtract their areas. For example, if a square has a circle inscribed in it and the shaded region is the area between the square and the circle, we would subtract the area of the circle from the area of the square. The key is to visualize the figure carefully, identify all relevant shapes, and apply the appropriate area formulas systematically.
points: Shaded regions are areas between geometric figures
Identify all shapes that make up the figure
Determine which areas to add and which to subtract
For area between square and inscribed circle: Subtract circle from square
For area between rectangle and semicircles: Add semicircles then subtract from rectangle
For overlapping circles: Find individual areas and subtract common area
Always draw clear diagrams to visualize the shaded region
Check if the answer is reasonable by estimating visually

keyTerms.meaning: The specific portion of a figure that is highlighted or colored
The mental or graphical representation of a geometric figure
The overlapping region shared by two or more figures
A step-by-step method for solving complex problems
An approximate calculation to check reasonableness of answer

sections.trick: Use 'Color Coding': Imagine different parts in different colors to identify what to add/subtract
sections.examPointer: CBSE commonly asks 4-6 mark questions on areas of shaded regions. These are typically multi-step problems requiring visualization and careful calculation. Always draw clear diagrams and show all steps of area calculations.

sections.heading: Real-Life Applications
sections.para: The concepts of areas related to circles have numerous real-life applications. In engineering, sector area calculations are used in designing gears, pulleys, and other circular components. In architecture, these concepts help in designing circular windows, arches, and domes. In agriculture, sector calculations are used to determine irrigation coverage for circular sprinkler systems. In sports, the area of a sector is used to design the playing fields of sports like baseball and cricket. Even in everyday life, understanding these concepts helps in calculating material needed for circular objects like tablecloths, pizza slices, or garden beds. These practical applications demonstrate the relevance of mathematical concepts in solving real-world problems.
points: Engineering applications in designing gears and pulleys
Architecture uses in designing circular windows and arches
Agriculture applications for irrigation systems
Sports field design using sector calculations
Everyday applications like pizza slice calculations
Landscaping for circular garden beds and fountains

Art and design involving circular patterns and segments

sections.examPointer: CBSE may include 1-2 mark application-based questions connecting circle areas to real-life scenarios. Focus on understanding how mathematical concepts apply to practical situations rather than just memorizing formulas.

sections.heading: Problem-Solving Strategies
sections.para: Effectively solving problems related to areas of circles requires a systematic approach. First, carefully read the problem and identify what is given and what is asked. Draw a clear diagram of the figure, labeling all known dimensions. Identify the relevant shapes and concepts needed to solve the problem. Apply the appropriate formulas systematically, showing all steps of calculation. Check your answer for reasonableness by estimation. For complex problems involving combinations of shapes, break them down into simpler components. Practice a variety of problems to develop proficiency. Remember to pay attention to units and ensure consistency throughout your calculations. Developing these problem-solving skills will help not only in this chapter but in mathematics as a whole.

Draw clear diagrams with labeled dimensions
Identify relevant shapes and applicable formulas

Check answers for reasonableness through estimation

sections.heading: Common Errors and Prevention
sections.para: Students often make certain errors when working on problems related to areas of circles. One common mistake is confusing the formulas for area of sector and area of segment. Remember that segment area requires subtracting the triangular portion from the sector area. Another frequent error is mixing up degree and radian measures in calculations. Always ensure consistency in units throughout the problem. Students also sometimes forget to include the radii in perimeter calculations, only calculating the arc length. Additionally, when working with combinations of shapes, errors often occur in identifying which areas to add and which to subtract. Careful visualization and diagram drawing can help prevent these mistakes. Regular practice and attention to detail will help minimize these errors.
points: Confusing sector and segment area formulas
Mixing degree and radian measures in calculations
Forgetting to include radii in perimeter calculations
Incorrectly identifying which areas to add/subtract in combinations
Using incorrect values of π (use 22/7 or π as specified)

mcqs.question: Which of the following is the correct statement about the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic?
options: Every composite number can be expressed as the product of primes in only one way
Every prime number can be expressed as the sum of two primes
Every natural number can be expressed as the sum of two primes
Every composite number can be expressed as the sum of primes
mcqs.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every composite number can be expressed as the product of primes in only one way, ignoring the order of primes.

mcqs.question: If the HCF of 12 and 15 is 3, then what is their LCM?
mcqs.explanation: LCM can be found using the formula: LCM(a,b) = (a*b)/HCF(a,b). So LCM(12,15) = (12*15)/3 = 60.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is an irrational number?
mcqs.explanation: sqrt(2) cannot be expressed as a ratio of two integers, making it irrational. The other options are perfect squares and hence rational.

mcqs.question: If the zeroes of the quadratic polynomial x^2 + 3x + k are equal, then what is the value of k?
mcqs.explanation: For equal zeroes, discriminant must be zero. Discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac = 9 - 4k = 0, so k = 9/4.

mcqs.question: For which value of k will the system of equations 2x + 3y = 5 and 4x + ky = 10 have infinitely many solutions?
mcqs.explanation: For infinitely many solutions, a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2. Here 2/4 = 3/k = 5/10, so k = 6.

mcqs.question: If the discriminant of a quadratic equation is negative, then the roots are:
mcqs.explanation: A negative discriminant means the quadratic has no real roots, only complex (imaginary) roots.

mcqs.question: The first term of an AP is 5 and the common difference is 3. What is the 10th term?
mcqs.explanation: Using the formula nth term = a + (n-1)d, we get 10th term = 5 + 9*3 = 32.

mcqs.question: In triangles ABC and DEF, if angle A = angle D and AB/DE = AC/DF, then the triangles are similar by which criterion?
mcqs.explanation: The SAS similarity criterion requires two sides in proportion and the included angle equal, which matches the given information.

mcqs.question: The coordinates of the midpoint of the line segment joining (2,3) and (4,5) are:
Which trigonometric identity is correct?
mcqs.explanation: The fundamental trigonometric identity is sin^2 A + cos^2 A = 1, which holds for all angles A.

mcqs.question: If the height of a tower is 10 sqrt(3) m and the angle of elevation of its top is 30 degrees, what is the distance from the observer to the foot of the tower?
mcqs.explanation: Using tan(30) = opposite/adjacent = height/distance, so distance = height/tan(30) = 10 sqrt(3)/(1/sqrt(3)) = 10 sqrt(3) m.

mcqs.question: A tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact. This statement is:
options: true only for circles with radius 1
true only for circles with radius greater than 1
mcqs.explanation: This is a fundamental property of circles that holds true for all circles regardless of their size.

mcqs.question: The area of a sector of a circle with radius 7 cm and angle 60 degrees is:
A cone of height 12 cm and radius 5 cm is placed on top of a hemisphere of the same radius. The total surface area is:
mcqs.explanation: Total surface area = curved surface of cone + curved surface of hemisphere = pi r l + 2 pi r^2 = pi * 5 * 13 + 2 pi * 25 = 65 pi + 50 pi = 115 pi cm^2.

mcqs.question: If the mean of 5, 7, 9, x, 11 is 8, then what is the value of x?
mcqs.explanation: Mean = sum of observations / number of observations. So (5+7+9+x+11)/5 = 8, giving x = 8.

mcqs.question: The empirical relation between mean, median and mode is:
mcqs.explanation: The empirical relationship is mode = 3 median - 2 mean, which holds for moderately skewed distributions.

mcqs.question: A bag contains 3 red and 5 blue balls. The probability of drawing a blue ball is:
mcqs.explanation: Probability of blue ball = number of blue balls / total balls = 5/8.

mcqs.question: The probability of an event is 0.6. What is the probability of its complementary event?
mcqs.explanation: The sum of probabilities of complementary events is 1, so P(complement) = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that sqrt(3) is irrational.
boardQuestions.answer: Assume sqrt(3) is rational, so sqrt(3) = p/q where p and q are coprime integers. Then 3 = p^2/q^2, so p^2 = 3q^2. This means p^2 is divisible by 3, hence p is divisible by 3 (since 3 is prime). Let p = 3k. Then (3k)^2 = 3q^2, so 9k^2 = 3q^2, thus 3k^2 = q^2. This means q^2 is divisible by 3, hence q is divisible by 3. But if both p and q are divisible by 3, they are not coprime, contradicting our assumption. Therefore, sqrt(3) must be irrational.

boardQuestions.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 12, 15 and 21 using prime factorization.
boardQuestions.answer: Prime factorization: 12 = 2^2 × 3^1, 15 = 3^1 × 5^1, 21 = 3^1 × 7^1. HCF is the product of lowest powers of common primes: 3^1 = 3. LCM is the product of highest powers of all primes: 2^2 × 3^1 × 5^1 × 7^1 = 4 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 420.

boardQuestions.question: Solve the quadratic equation 2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 0 by factorization method.
boardQuestions.answer: We need to find two numbers that multiply to 2×3=6 and add to -5. These numbers are -2 and -3. So 2x^2 - 5x + 3 = 2x^2 - 2x - 3x + 3 = 2x(x - 1) - 3(x - 1) = (2x - 3)(x - 1) = 0. Therefore, x = 3/2 or x = 1.

boardQuestions.question: For what value of k will the following pair of linear equations have infinitely many solutions? 2x + 3y = 7 and (k + 1)x + (2k - 1)y = 4k + 1.
boardQuestions.answer: For infinitely many solutions, a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2. So 2/(k+1) = 3/(2k-1) = 7/(4k+1). From 2/(k+1) = 3/(2k-1), we get 2(2k-1) = 3(k+1), so 4k - 2 = 3k + 3, thus k = 5. Checking with the third ratio: 7/(4×5+1) = 7/21 = 1/3, and 2/(5+1) = 2/6 = 1/3, which matches. So k = 5.

boardQuestions.question: The sum of first n terms of an AP is given by S_n = 3n^2 + 5n. Find the 10th term of this AP.
In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B, if tan A = 3/4, find sin A and cos A.
boardQuestions.answer: Given tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB = 3/4. Let BC = 3k and AB = 4k. Using Pythagoras theorem, AC = sqrt(BC^2 + AB^2) = sqrt((3k)^2 + (4k)^2) = sqrt(9k^2 + 16k^2) = sqrt(25k^2) = 5k. Therefore, sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC = 3k/5k = 3/5, and cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AB/AC = 4k/5k = 4/5.

boardQuestions.question: Prove that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
boardQuestions.answer: Let O be the center of the circle and P be an external point. Let PA and PB be the two tangents from P to the circle, touching at points A and B respectively. Join OA and OB. Since PA is tangent to the circle at A, angle OAP = 90°. Similarly, angle OBP = 90°. In triangles OAP and OBP, OA = OB (radii of the same circle), OP is common, and angle OAP = angle OBP = 90°. Therefore, by RHS congruence criterion, triangles OAP and OBP are congruent. Hence, PA = PB, proving that the lengths of tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.

boardQuestions.question: A solid toy is in the form of a hemisphere surmounted by a right circular cone. The height of the cone is 4 cm and the diameter of the base is 6 cm. Find the volume of the toy.
boardQuestions.answer: Given diameter = 6 cm, so radius r = 3 cm. Height of cone h = 4 cm. Volume of toy = volume of hemisphere + volume of cone. Volume of hemisphere = (2/3)πr^3 = (2/3)π(3)^3 = (2/3)π(27) = 18π cm^3. Volume of cone = (1/3)πr^2h = (1/3)π(3)^2(4) = (1/3)π(9)(4) = 12π cm^3. Total volume = 18π + 12π = 30π cm^3. Using π = 22/7, volume = 30 × 22/7 = 660/7 cm^3.

boardQuestions.question: The mean of the following distribution is 53. Find the value of f: Class: 0-20, 20-40, 40-60, 60-80, 80-100 Frequency: 15, f, 21, 17, 9
boardQuestions.answer: First, we calculate the mid-points (x) of each class: 10, 30, 50, 70, 90. We know mean = Σ(fx)/Σf = 53. Σf = 15 + f + 21 + 17 + 9 = 62 + f. Σ(fx) = 15×10 + f×30 + 21×50 + 17×70 + 9×90 = 150 + 30f + 1050 + 1190 + 810 = 3200 + 30f. So 53 = (3200 + 30f)/(62 + f). Cross-multiplying: 53(62 + f) = 3200 + 30f, so 3286 + 53f = 3200 + 30f. Rearranging: 53f - 30f = 3200 - 3286, so 23f = -86, thus f = -86/23 = -4. Since frequency cannot be negative, there must be an error in the calculation. Let's recheck: Σ(fx) = 15×10 + f×30 + 21×50 + 17×70 + 9×90 = 150 + 30f + 1050 + 1190 + 810 = 3200 + 30f. Σf = 15 + f + 21 + 17 + 9 = 62 + f. So 53(62 + f) = 3200 + 30f, 3286 + 53f = 3200 + 30f, 23f = -86, f = -4. This negative value suggests there might be an error in the problem statement or mean value given.

boardQuestions.question: A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards. Find the probability that it is: (i) a red card, (ii) a king, (iii) a red king, (iv) not a face card.
boardQuestions.answer: Total cards = 52. (i) Number of red cards = 26 (13 hearts + 13 diamonds). P(red) = 26/52 = 1/2. (ii) Number of kings = 4. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. (iii) Number of red kings = 2 (king of hearts and king of diamonds). P(red king) = 2/52 = 1/26. (iv) Number of face cards = 12 (4 kings + 4 queens + 4 jacks). Number of non-face cards = 52 - 12 = 40. P(not face card) = 40/52 = 10/13.
